---
title: "Quiz: lifetimes, decays and photon counting"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Times in ns; 80 MHz means a laser pulse every 12.5 ns.

---

**Q1.** A cell is twice as bright as its neighbour, but both show the same lifetime. A third cell has the same brightness as the first, but its lifetime fell from 2.5 to 1.5 ns. Which observation points to a change in the molecules' surroundings?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which of the two numbers depends on how many molecules there are?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The third cell. Twice the brightness at the same lifetime is most simply twice as many molecules (or a brighter illumination). A shorter lifetime means a new way for the excited molecules to lose their energy: quenching, binding, FRET. Intensity alone could not have told the two cases apart.
:::

---

**Q2.** τ = 2 ns. Which fraction of the photons arrives later than 2 ns after the pulse? Later than 6 ns?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The fraction still to come at time $t$ is $e^{-t/\tau}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$e^{-1} = 37\,\%$ after one lifetime, $e^{-3} = 5\,\%$ after three.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does a time-correlated single-photon counting system detect a photon in only a few percent of the laser pulses?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens when two photons arrive after the same pulse?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The electronics time only the first photon after a pulse. If photons often came in pairs, the later ones would be lost, early arrival times would be over-counted and the lifetime would look too short (pile-up). Keeping the rate at a few percent makes pairs rare (at 1 % of pulses, 0.5 % of them hold a second photon). The price is speed.
:::

---

**Q4.** The instrument response function (IRF) is to the time axis what ... is to the image? What does it do to the measured decay?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Recall [the forward model](../psf/lec.qmd) of the image formation day.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The PSF. The measured histogram is the true decay **convolved** with the IRF (plus a flat background and Poisson noise): the sharp start of the decay is blurred and delayed by the IRF's width and position.
:::

---

**Q5.** The measured mean arrival time of a pixel is 3.4 ns, and the IRF's mean is 0.9 ns. Estimate τ. Name one thing that would make this estimate wrong.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Means add under convolution.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
τ ≈ 3.4 − 0.9 = 2.5 ns. It is wrong with a flat background (pulls the mean towards the middle of the window), with τ not much shorter than the period (the tail wraps into the next period), with pile-up, or with two lifetimes (then it gives an average, not either one).
:::

---

**Q6.** Why does a lifetime of 8 ns cause trouble at 80 MHz, but 1 ns does not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How much of the decay is still to come when the next pulse fires?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The next pulse comes after 12.5 ns. For τ = 8 ns, $e^{-12.5/8} = 21\,\%$ of the decay is still to come: its photons land in the next period (wrap-around), and the histogram is a sum over earlier pulses. For τ = 1 ns only $e^{-12.5} \approx 4 \cdot 10^{-6}$ is left.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why show a lifetime image with hue = lifetime and brightness = intensity, rather than the lifetime alone?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How reliable is the lifetime of a pixel with 5 photons?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Dim pixels have few photons, so their lifetimes are very noisy (and background pixels have no meaningful lifetime at all). Weighting the colour by intensity fades them to black, so the eye sees the lifetime where it is reliable and the structure of the cell at the same time.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that for $I(t) = Ae^{-t/\tau}$ and two adjacent gates of width Δt, $D_1/D_2 = e^{\Delta t/\tau}$ wherever the first gate starts.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Substitute $t = u + \Delta t$ in the second integral.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$D_2 = \int_{a + \Delta t}^{a + 2\Delta t} Ae^{-t/\tau}dt = \int_a^{a + \Delta t} Ae^{-(u + \Delta t)/\tau}du = e^{-\Delta t/\tau}D_1$. So $D_1/D_2 = e^{\Delta t/\tau}$, independent of $a$ and $A$: hence $\tau = \Delta t/\ln(D_1/D_2)$.
:::
